aiSummary: Speckled trout and redfish are the dominant story on Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with recent reports from late July 2026 confirming plentiful trout scattered across the bay and bull redfish showing up in impressive numbers — including fish over 26 lbs. Today's conditions are classic summer: mostly sunny with an 85°F water temperature, light SSE wind building to 10 mph, and a low-probability storm window (13%) that closes after 4 PM. Get on the water at or before first light to beat the heat and make the most of the outgoing tide running toward the 11:32 AM low.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans a narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides and concentrates speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around the pilings year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on an incoming tide, while the funnel effect makes this spot productive on either tide direction. It is the most exposed location on this dashboard — open water and chop make it the first spot to become unfishable when wind builds.
bridge.todaysCall: The tide bottoms out at 11:32 AM and begins its push back toward the high at 11:42 PM, so the best window here is the couple of hours on either side of that low — bait will be funneling through the pilings as the tide transitions. SSE wind at 0–10 mph today is light enough to keep the open water fishable, but position on the lee side of the pilings to stay comfortable and keep your presentation in the strike zone. Bright sun and slightly stained water favor darker or chartreuse soft plastics worked tight to the structure. Wrap up before the early-afternoon hours given the 13% storm chance before 4 PM, and the heat will be building significantly by midday at 91°F anyway — an early start is strongly advisable.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus speckled trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime structure, and tree cover keeps the interior a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing natural shelter from wind. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and can hold largemouth bass alongside small redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Tree cover and interior protection make Alaqua a smart choice on a bright, hot summer day — you'll get some shade on the upper creek and the slightly cooler water can keep fish active longer into the morning. Work the oyster bars at the mouth during the moving tide: the outgoing flow running toward the 11:32 AM low will be concentrating baitfish on the bar edges through mid-morning, a prime window for redfish and trout. Slightly stained water pairs well with darker or gold-colored soft plastics and weedless rigs worked along the oyster edges. The 13% storm chance before 4 PM is low but real — being in protected water here means you're well positioned to ride out any afternoon pop-up if one develops.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees lighter pressure than Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to mean less-pressured, more cooperative fish. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally appear at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It is less protected than LaGrange when weather builds, though the interior flats still offer reasonable shelter in light-wind conditions.
basin.todaysCall: Light SSE wind at 0–10 mph and mostly sunny skies set up well for sight-fishing the interior grass flats for redfish in skinny water — polarized glasses are essential and an early push gets you on the flat before the sun angle goes high and fish push deeper or into shade. The outgoing tide heading toward the 11:32 AM low will pull water off the flats, so plan to be on the interior grass early and transition toward the creek mouth as the tide drops and fish follow the moving water. Slightly stained water reduces visibility a bit for sight-casting but redfish in shallow grass are still very findable; try weedless gold spoons or soft plastics in natural shrimp colors. With the storm window closing by 4 PM and low probability at 13%, you have a solid morning-into-early-afternoon run available — just don't push past early afternoon in this less-protected water.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is the top trout producer on this dashboard, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside the bayou harbor black drum and sheepshead, rounding out one of the most species-diverse inshore spots in the area. It is the most protected water on its side of the bay, making it the default choice when weather builds.
lagrange.todaysCall: Recent late-July reports put speckled trout actively feeding across the bay, and LaGrange's oyster bar mouth is as likely a concentration point as anywhere — plan to work those bars hard during the outgoing tide window before the 11:32 AM low, then reassess as the tide transitions and fish shift position. Bright sun and slightly stained water suggest going subsurface with paddle-tail soft plastics or a popping cork rig over the bars rather than relying on surface lures once the sun gets high. The protected nature of this bayou is a genuine advantage today: even if the SSE breeze builds toward 10 mph, you'll have comfortable fishing, and if the 13% storm chance produces anything before 4 PM, LaGrange is the right place to be. An early start — on the water by or just after the 6:04 AM sunrise — is strongly recommended to maximize the cool hours and the best light conditions for reading the flats.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where incoming tides push baitfish up the creek and concentrate redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The upper section transitions to brackish water and holds largemouth bass alongside small redfish, while the creek mouth is a recognized flounder zone. It is short, sheltered, and considered the safest fishery on this dashboard when weather threatens.
fourmile.todaysCall: Today's tide pattern makes the transition window around the 11:32 AM low worth planning around — the incoming tide that follows will push bait up into the creek, which is exactly when Four Mile fishes best for reds and trout stacking in the bends. Arrive early to work the creek mouth for flounder on the tail end of the outgoing, then stay positioned for the tide flip. With SSE wind at 0–10 mph and a low storm risk (13% before 4 PM), conditions are benign, but Four Mile's enclosed character means you're well protected regardless. Slightly stained water favors slow-rolled soft plastics or live shrimp near grass edges and bend drop-offs — keep presentations close to structure where fish are holding in the warmer water.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide spot and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay, with summer mornings considered the peak season as trout stack on grass flats in two to four feet of water. Spanish mackerel appear at the mouth on moving tides, adding a bonus target. It sits further from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous on this dashboard, so factor in run time when planning your trip.
hogtown.todaysCall: Summer morning trout on the grass flats is exactly the pattern that's been producing bay-wide in recent reports, and Hogtown is one of the best addresses for it — be on the flat well before the sun gets high, ideally right around the 6:04 AM sunrise, to catch trout actively feeding before the 91°F heat pushes fish deeper. The outgoing tide running toward the 11:32 AM low will be moving water across the grass in two to four feet, a textbook setup; work popping corks or weedless paddle-tails along flat edges and any subtle depth changes you can find. Spanish mackerel are a bonus possibility at the mouth during that moving tide — keep a faster-moving lure or spoon rigged as a second option. Account for the longer run time from the 331 Bridge area in your timing, and be off open water or headed back well before any early-afternoon weather develops given the storm window before 4 PM.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary feeding directly into LaGrange Bayou — this dashboard's top trout producer — just south of Freeport. That direct connection means the productive oyster-bar redfish and trout pattern that defines LaGrange plausibly extends into this smaller, quieter water, though there is far less documented fishing history for Mallet specifically. Its small, interior character makes it a likely calm-water option when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Think of Mallet as a quieter, lower-pressure extension of the LaGrange bite — if the oyster bars at LaGrange's mouth are seeing competition from other anglers, slide up into Mallet for the same basic redfish-and-trout pattern with fewer boats. Work the outgoing tide toward the 11:32 AM low and focus on any oyster or grass structure you can find near the connection point with LaGrange. Slightly stained water and bright sun suggest soft plastics in natural or charteuse colors fished slow along bottom or structure edges. With light SSE wind and a manageable storm risk (13% before 4 PM), today is a fine day to explore this less-documented water — just temper expectations slightly given the limited fishing record compared to its larger neighbor.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a genuine long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares the protected-bayou character of Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees less pressure simply because of its distance from the main boat ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: The distance commitment is real, so plan an early departure — on the water at or before the 6:04 AM sunrise puts you at Mack Bayou during the cooler, low-light hours that are most productive in summer, and you'll be working the outgoing tide toward the 11:32 AM low during prime feeding time on arrival. Lighter pressure here means redfish and trout that are less educated about lures — a genuine edge on a summer day when pressured fish can be lockjawed by mid-morning. Oyster bars and marsh grass edges are your primary targets with soft plastics or weedless gold spoons. The 13% storm chance before 4 PM is worth keeping in mind given the long return run — be watching conditions and start heading back well before early afternoon if the sky starts building to the east.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in the same trip. The habitat mirrors its neighbors — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth, deeper interior holes further in — and it sees light pressure due to its distance from the main launch ramps. Like Mack, it is a long-run destination from the 331 Bridge area.
hewett.todaysCall: Pair Hewett with Mack Bayou for an efficient long-run day: hit one on the outgoing tide in the morning and work the other as the tide transitions around the 11:32 AM low. Oyster bars at the mouth are the priority on any moving water; interior holes are worth probing if the exterior bars go quiet once the sun is fully up and the tide slackens. Slightly stained water favors slightly larger or more visible profile baits — a chartreuse or white paddle-tail on a light jig head works well along the bar edges. The same weather caution applies as for Mack: a 13% storm probability before 4 PM is not alarming, but the long run home makes it prudent to start back earlier than you think you need to.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should track its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak confidently about it specifically. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: If you're already running to Mack and Hewett, Buck Bayou is a worthwhile quick stop — probe the mouth structure and any visible grass or oyster edges on the moving tide and move on if you don't find fish within 20–30 minutes. Keep expectations calibrated given limited documentation, but the same redfish and trout pattern that drives its neighbors is the logical target. Today's light SSE wind and low storm risk make the long run feasible, though as with any of the 30-A bayous, keep a close eye on the sky and plan to be heading home well before early afternoon given the storm window before 4 PM and the distance involved.
